extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students in probability theory or measure-theoretic probability
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of characteristic-function techniques, moment problems, and central limit theorems (i.i.d. and triangular arrays) including precise conditions, error bounds, and representative examples and exercises. Useful for proving CLTs and checking hypotheses (moments, Lindeberg/Lyapunov conditions, uniqueness of moment problem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of derivatives of characteristic function (Theorem 3.3.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫ |x|^n μ(dx) < ∞ then its characteristic function ϕ has a continuous derivative of order n given by ϕ^{(n)}(t) = ∫ (i x)^n e^{itx} μ(dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by repeatedly differentiating under the integral and using justification (Theorem A.5.1). In particular, existence of finite n-th absolute moment implies n-times differentiability (and gives explicit formula for derivatives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor expansion of characteristic function around 0
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X|^n < ∞ then ϕ(t) = Σ_{m=0}^n E((itX)^m)/m! + o(t^n) as t→0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The o(t^n) remainder is made precise via Lemma 3.3.19 and bound (3.3.3); estimating the error term is important for CLT proofs and allows control without higher moments in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remainder bound for e^{ix} Taylor expansion (Lemma 3.3.19 / inequality (3.3.2))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First term is the usual (small x) order; second is better for large |x| and is used to prove CLT without assuming finite third moments. Proof via repeated integration by parts; use |e^{is}| ≤ 1 and |e^{ix}-1| ≤ 2 to obtain the two bounds and combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected-value remainder bound for characteristic functions (inequality (3.3.3))
rubrics_metrics.description: E[e^{itX}] - Σ_{m=0}^n E((itX)^m)/m!  has absolute value ≤ E[ min( |tX|^{n+1}/(n+1)!,  2|tX|^n / n! ) ], and (for simplicity) ≤ E[ min( |tX|^{n+1}, 2|tX|^n ) ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This converts pointwise Taylor remainder bounds into expectation bounds, allowing control of the CF expansion under moment conditions weaker than existence of the (n+1)-st moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-order expansion under finite second moment (Theorem 3.3.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X|^2 < ∞ then ϕ(t) = 1 + it E X - t^2 E(X^2)/2 + o(t^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error term is ≤ t^2 E( |t|·|X|^3 ∧ 2|X|^2 ). Since the parenthesized variable is ≤ 2|X|^2 and tends to 0 as t→0, dominated convergence gives o(t^2). Crucially, finite second moment suffices (no third moment assumed) because of the min-type remainder bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using min-type remainder to avoid higher-moment assumptions (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The min(|x|^{n+1}/(n+1)!, 2|x|^n/n!) form yields conclusions (e.g., Theorem 3.3.20) under weaker hypotheses than naive Taylor: e.g., second-order CF expansion under only E|X|^2 < ∞ (no need for E|X|^3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly points out the importance of the second term in the remainder bound for treating large |x| and avoiding extra moment assumptions in CLT proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-difference behaviour implies second moment existence (Theorem 3.3.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim sup_{h↓0} { ϕ(h) - 2ϕ(0) + ϕ(-h) } / h^2 > -∞ then E|X|^2 < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: relate (e^{ihx} - 2 + e^{-ihx})/h^2 = -2(1 - cos(hx))/h^2 ≤ 0 and 2(1 - cos(hx))/h^2 → x^2 as h→0; apply Fatou and Fubini to conclude ∫ x^2 dF(x) < ∞. This ties differentiability/second-difference control of CF to actual finiteness of second moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tightness implies equicontinuity of characteristic functions (Exercise 3.3.13(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a family of measures {μ_i} is tight (sup_i μ_i([−M,M]^c) → 0 as M→∞) then their characteristic functions ϕ_i are equicontinuous: for any ε>0 there exists δ>0 so that |h|<δ implies |ϕ_i(t+h) - ϕ_i(t)| < ε for all i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decomposition and the bound (3.3.3) with n=0; equicontinuity is then used (with convergence of CFs) to get uniform convergence on compacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's criterion for being a characteristic function (Theorem 3.3.22)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ϕ(t) is real nonnegative with ϕ(0)=1, ϕ(t)=ϕ(−t), and ϕ is decreasing and convex on (0,∞) with lim_{t↓0}ϕ(t)=1 and lim_{t↑∞}ϕ(t)=0, then there exists a probability measure ν on (0,∞) so that ϕ(t) = ∫_0^∞ (1 - (|t|/s)+) ν(ds), hence ϕ is a characteristic function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct ν from the right derivative ϕ' and show representation (∗). The representation expresses ϕ as a convex combination of known CFs (Example 3.3.15), so extension arguments and approximation by atomic measures give the full result. Remarks note necessity of lim_{t→0}ϕ(t)=1 and possible extensions with mass at 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable-type CF exp(−|t|^α) is a characteristic function for 0<α≤2 (Example 3.3.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: exp(−|t|^α) is a characteristic function for 0<α<2 (and α=2 gives the normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches: (i) for 0<α≤1 use Polya's criterion; (ii) extend to 0<α<2 by series expansion/representation and limits (construct ψ with nonnegative coefficients and use limit theorems on CFs). For α>2 it fails (Exercise 3.3.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of distribution from moments under growth condition (Theorem 3.3.25)
rubrics_metrics.description: If lim sup_{k→∞} μ_{2k}^{1/2k} / (2k) = r < ∞ then there is at most one distribution function F with moments μ_k = ∫ x^k dF(x) for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a sufficient condition for determinacy of the Hamburger moment problem (slightly stronger than Carleman's condition). Proof uses bounds on moment growth to get analytic continuation domain for the characteristic function's Taylor series, then uniqueness of CF on an interval implies equality of distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence from moment convergence plus growth control (Theorem 3.3.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∫ x^k dF_n(x) → μ_k for each k and lim sup μ_{2k}^{1/2k} / (2k) < ∞ then F_n converges weakly to the unique distribution with those moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine tightness (from uniform control on moments) with the uniqueness result (Theorem 3.3.25) to deduce weak convergence to the unique moment-determined limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: i.i.d. Central Limit Theorem via characteristic functions (Theorem 3.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_i be i.i.d. with EX_i = μ and var(X_i) = σ^2 ∈ (0,∞). If S_n = X_1 + ... + X_n then (S_n - nμ)/(σ √n) ⇒ standard normal χ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: reduce to zero mean, expand CF ϕ(t)=1 - σ^2 t^2/2 + o(t^2), then ϕ(t/σ√n)^n → exp(−t^2/2) by (complex) limit (Theorem 3.4.2), and apply Lévy continuity theorem (Theorem 3.3.17).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex exponential limit (Theorem 3.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If c_n → c ∈ C then (1 + c_n/n)^n → e^c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Lemmas 3.4.3 (product-difference bound for complex numbers with modulus ≤ θ) and 3.4.4 (|e^b - (1+b)| ≤ |b|^2 for |b|≤1) to control differences between products and exponentials in the complex plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindeberg-Feller central limit theorem for triangular arrays (Theorem 3.4.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each n, let X_{n,m}, 1≤m≤n, be independent with EX_{n,m}=0. Suppose (i) Σ_{m=1}^n EX_{n,m}^2 → σ^2 > 0 and (ii) for all ε>0, Σ_{m=1}^n E( |X_{n,m}|^2 ; |X_{n,m}| > ε ) → 0. Then S_n = Σ_{m=1}^n X_{n,m} ⇒ N(0,σ^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: sum of many small independent effects approximates a normal distribution. The proof uses CF approximations with remainder bound (3.3.3), product control (Lemma 3.4.3), and the fact that sup_m Var(X_{n,m})→0 so individual terms are small. This contains the i.i.d. CLT as a special case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lindeberg criterion specialization: smallness of maximal variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in the proof is that Lindeberg condition (ii) forces sup_m Var(X_{n,m}) → 0 and ensures the product expansion converges to exp(−t^2 σ^2/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation is used to validate approximation by (1 − t^2 σ^2_{n,m}/2) factors and then exponentiate the sum to get the Gaussian CF; it explains why no single large summand can dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyapunov condition for CLT (Exercise 3.4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let α_n = sqrt{Var(S_n)}. If there exists δ>0 such that lim_{n→∞} α_n^{-(2+δ)} Σ_{m=1}^n E( |X_m - EX_m|^{2+δ} ) = 0 then (S_n - E S_n)/α_n ⇒ standard normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyapunov's condition is a stronger but simpler-to-check sufficient condition than Lindeberg's; the exercise indicates this as a standard sufficient criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and sufficient tail/variance balance for normalization to normal (Theorem 3.4.14, Lévý)
rubrics_metrics.description: For i.i.d. X_i, there exist normalizing constants a_n and b_n>0 so that (S_n - a_n)/b_n ⇒ normal if and only if y^2 P(|X_1|>y) / E( |X_1|^2 ; |X_1| ≤ y ) → 0 as y→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the exact tail/variance balance required for normalization to produce a Gaussian limit; proof referenced to Gnedenko and Kolmogorov (1954).

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular-array truncation method (Second proof structure of Lindeberg-Feller)
rubrics_metrics.description: One may truncate X_{n,m} at a sequence ε_n→0 to split each term into a large-tail part and a bounded part. Show large-tail contribution is negligible in L2 and then handle bounded part via moment computations to get Gaussian moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 3.4.15 constructs ε_n so that h_n(ε_n)→0; then define truncated variables and show difference tends to 0 in L2; compute moments of truncated sums and use combinatorial moment evaluation to match Gaussian moments. This is the technical route followed in the chapter's second proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application: Erdős–Kac theorem strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Model number-of-prime-divisors function g(n) as sum of indicators δ_p(n) and approximate by independent Bernoulli variables X_p with P(X_p=1)=1/p for primes p up to α_n (chosen appropriately). Use bn = Σ_{p≤α_n} 1/p and variance a_n^2 = Σ_{p≤α_n} 1/p(1-1/p) (both ≈ log log n) and apply triangular-array CLT to get normal approximation for (g(n) - log log n)/(log log n)^{1/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key preparatory facts: Σ_{p≤n} 1/p = log log n + O(1) and Σ 1/p^2 < ∞. Choose α_n = n^{1/ log log n} so contribution from large primes is negligible. This gives the heuristic and rigorous path to Erdős–Kac in this chapter.
